steps.name: chat.expectTriggerFired
steps.description: Assert that a github-event TRIGGER woke this agent, observed on the session SSE stream (#711 — "trigger fired = the agent's chat shows the trigger event via SSE"). The runtime appends a `trigger.fired` event to the session log at the head of every triggered run (agent-entrypoint.py `_execute_inner`); we subscribe to that agent's session stream from byte 0 and resolve on it. Self- contained: resolves the agent's DM room id itself (the trigger posts there), so the journey YAML only names the agentId. The stream endpoint holds the connection open even before the log file exists, so subscribing right after applying the label is safe (no lost event, no sleep).

params.name: agentId
params.description: Id of the agent expected to be woken by the trigger.

params.name: timeoutMs
params.description: Max time to wait for the trigger.fired event.

steps.name: chat.waitForAgentReady
steps.description: Wait until the agent's RUNTIME is demonstrably up before sending the first message. The runtime drops any m.room.message whose origin_server_ts predates its own process start (agent-entrypoint.py, `ts < start_time_ms`) — so a send that races the container boot is silently ignored BY DESIGN, and F2 would time out without any product bug. `/api/agents/statuses` flips the agent from `offline` to `idle` exactly when the runtime has booted and pushed its status.json (#185) — after that point, a fresh message is inside the processing contract. Bounded poll, no sleeps beyond the interval tick.

params.name: agentId
params.description: Id of the agent whose runtime to wait for.

params.name: timeoutMs
params.description: Max time to wait for readiness.

fixtures.name: contextMountAgent
fixtures.description: contextMountAgent: the context-mount journey's precondition (#1319). KIND-LANE ONLY — the mount is a k8s hostPath, so "host" is the kind node container: setup shells into it (docker/podman exec from the Playwright host, the same engine that runs the kind provider) to seed the folder, then stands up one standalone agent on a repo-less env and sets a READ-WRITE multi-folder context mount via the real PATCH route (#1290 shape — the folder gets a slug and mounts at /context/<slug> in the agent pod). The agent is enabled last; the journey's first browse poll absorbs the pod startup window. ENSURE, NEVER DELETE: deleting an agent deactivates its Matrix user, and a conduwuit deactivation is permanent — recreating the same fixed id then fails with M_USER_DEACTIVATED. So setup treats an existing agent/env as reusable (409 = fine) and teardown only DISABLES the agent (pod gone, node folder removable) — same lifecycle as stack-up.sh's standalone e2e-agent. The pre-clean also disables first: re-seeding the node folder while a live pod bind-mounts it would leave that pod staring at the deleted inode.

It mints two real user-store records with local passwords (#374/#1844) and signs each one in through the real `/api/auth/login` into its own browser context, registered as `owner` and `colleague`. Steps then point the journey's ctx at one of them with `access.actAs` — which re-points the whole existing step library, and the screenshot recorder with it, at that human. It deliberately creates NO team: "user A creates a team" is the journey's own first beat, and it has to run as A for #2081 to record A as its Team Admin. Teardown ORDER is load-bearing: the team (and its auto-created environment) goes first, because #2081's D4 rule refuses to delete a human who is still the last Team Admin of any team — and deleting the team is what cascades the memberships that would otherwise pin its members in place forever. The same order runs on setup as a pre-clean, so a crashed prior run cannot wedge the next one. Browser contexts are closed last, and the primary `page`/`request` fixtures are restored before they are.
